---
title: "Change of Basis — Same Arrow, Different Coordinates"
description: "A compact linear-algebra lesson with mathematical definitions, real values and reasoning."
---

## Start with a question

A visitor describes a city route using east/north, while a local describes it using two diagonal street directions. Is one of them wrong?

## Understand the central idea

A basis is a coordinate language. The vector itself stays fixed even if its numbers change.

## Express it with mathematics

$$
[\mathbf v]_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}\mathbf v
$$

**Every symbol explained:** [v]_B means coordinates of geometric vector v in basis B; B is the matrix whose columns are the new basis directions, and B^-1 is its inverse. The formula assumes B is square and invertible.

**Substitute real numbers:** Use new basis b1=(1,1), b2=(1,−1). Then B=[[1,1],[1,−1]]. For v=(4,2), solve 4=a+b and 2=a−b, giving a=3,b=1. So the same vector has new-basis coordinates (3,1).

## Why this works

The equation B[v]_B=v says that combining the new basis arrows with the new coordinates reproduces the original vector. Multiplying by B^-1 recovers the coordinates from standard ones.

## What can go wrong?

The numeric pair (3,1) is not the vector (4,2) written in the same coordinate system. Confusing coordinate values with physical vectors leads to mistakes in graphics and robotics.

## Your turn

Express (2,0) in the diagonal basis; check your result by recombining b1 and b2.
